hints: Hint 1: For translational equilibrium, consider what the vector sum of all forces acting on the object must be.
Hint 2: For rotational equilibrium, consider what the sum of all moments about any point must be.
teacher_walkthrough: The condition for translational equilibrium is that the resultant force on the object is zero in any direction.
The condition for rotational equilibrium is that the resultant moment or torque on the object about any point is zero.
walkthrough: B1: resultant force (in any direction) is zero.
B1: resultant moment / torque (about any point) is zero.
common_pitfalls: Stating only that forces are balanced or equal without stating resultant force is zero loses the mark.
Stating that moments are equal in both directions without stating resultant moment is zero is insufficient.
Confusing equilibrium with stationary, an object can be in equilibrium while moving at constant velocity.

hints: Hint 1: Resolve the 17 N tension using the 50 degree angle to the horizontal, with vertical component opposite the angle so use sine.
teacher_walkthrough: Resolution of a force at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal gives vertical component $$F_v = T \sin\theta$$
Substitute $T = 17 \text{ N}$ and $\theta = 50^{\circ}$: $$F_v = 17 \sin 50^{\circ}$$
Rounded to two significant figures this is $13 \text{ N}$, as required.
common_pitfalls: Using cosine instead of sine gives the horizontal component, about 10.9 N, not the vertical component.
Calculator in radian mode gives an incorrect value for sin 50 degrees.

hints: Hint 1: Take moments about A so hinge force has zero moment. Identify perpendicular distances: beam weight W acts at its centre 0.25 m from A, 12 N block acts at 0.35 m from A, 13 N vertical tension acts at 0.50 m from A.
Hint 2: Set sum of clockwise moments equal to sum of anticlockwise moments: W x 0.25 + 12 x 0.35 = 13 x 0.50, then solve for W.
teacher_walkthrough: The principle of moments for equilibrium about A is that sum of clockwise moments equals sum of anticlockwise moments.
Weight $W$ of uniform beam acts at centre: $$d_W = \frac{0.50}{2} = 0.25 \text{ m from A}$$
Block distance from A is: $$d_{block} = 0.50 - 0.15 = 0.35 \text{ m from A}$$
Vertical tension acts at B: $$d_T = 0.50 \text{ m from A}$$
Moment equation about A: $$(W \times 0.25) + (12 \times 0.35) = (13 \times 0.50)$$
Evaluate moments: $$13 \times 0.50 = 6.50 \text{ N m}$$ $$12 \times 0.35 = 4.20 \text{ N m}$$
common_pitfalls: Using 0.15 m as the block distance from A instead of 0.35 m from A.
Using full 17 N tension in the moment instead of the 13 N vertical component, only the perpendicular component gives a moment about A.

hints: Hint 1: Apply vertical force equilibrium: upward forces from tension and possibly hinge must balance downward weights W and 12 N.
teacher_walkthrough: Vertical equilibrium requires resultant vertical force is zero: $$\sum F_v = 0$$
Let $F_H$ be vertical hinge force. Take upward as positive: $$F_H + 13 - W - 12 = 0$$
Rearrange: $$F_H = W + 12 - 13$$
Magnitude is $8.2 \text{ N}$ (about $8 \text{ N}$ with rounding).
common_pitfalls: Sign error giving hinge force as 13 + 9.2 + 12 instead of balancing up against down.
Using 17 N instead of 13 N vertical component in the force balance.

hints: Hint 1: Consider how moving the block toward A changes its moment about A and hence the tension needed in the string to keep the moment balance, then link tension to its horizontal component.
teacher_walkthrough: Moment of block about A is $12 \times d$ where $d$ decreases as block moves toward A.
From $\sum M_A = 0$, smaller clockwise moment requires smaller anticlockwise moment from tension, so tension $T$ decreases.
Horizontal hinge force balances horizontal tension $T \cos 50^{\circ}$, so if $T$ decreases then $T \cos 50^{\circ}$ decreases.
Therefore horizontal component of hinge force decreases.
common_pitfalls: Stating no effect on the grounds that horizontal forces are independent of vertical positions.
Stating increase by confusing reduced load moment with increased hinge load.
